VIEW OF THE NATION

TV magazine in Britain has recently carried out a survey of
A viewing habits of the nation, and the results are
sometimes predictable, sometimes surprising and, it must
be said, a little worrying.
The findings are interesting but full of contradictions. For example,
in 40% of the homes that took part in the survey, the television is
on for more than six hours a day but only 12% of us admit to
watching it for that length of time. Why? Well, we call people who
watch TV for more than six hours a day “heavy viewers"; this is
quite a negative comment and it suggests we do not approve of
those who spend so much time in front of the TV every day.
Television is a necessity without which 54% would feel lonely.
This is an even more worrying statistic when we see that 48% of
the viewers of this 54% do not live alone. What has happened to
the art of conversation? Maybe it isn’t dead yet. The survey asked
people what they regularly did while watching TV and more than half
said that they talked to family and friends or made a phone call.
Others admitted that they did the housework, read, cooked or had a
snack. Doesn't anyone just watch the programme? Only viewers
over the age of 55 concentrate on programmes; younger viewers
watch it with just one eye so that they can complete other tasks
at the same time.

Not surprisingly, the survey highlighted differences between men
and women. Women like drama; men prefer to watch the news
and current. affairs programmes. At the top of a woman's list is
her favourite soap and at the bottom is sport. Men place sport
at the top and soaps at the bottom! Three times more women
than men watch reality TV. So, is TV a barrier between the sexes?
It seems so.
We think that a TV is in our home to entertain us but it now has
other functions. 67% of parents use the TV to occupy the children
when they are busy and 36% of kids have a TV in their bedroom.
However, nearly half of adults believe that there is too much
violence on TV, and that many cartoons are too violent for children
to watch, It is not unusual for childreh to do their homework while

Children sit in front of the TV for about three hours a day and, on
average, British TVs are switched on for five hours each day. Each
home has 2.21 TV sets but 72% say that there are many similar

enough that reflect European lifestyles.
We want better programmes but we just get more channels.
Despite these complaints about what our TV channels broadcast,
television is everything to us. It has many defects, but we rarely
turn it off. We hate it, but we watch it and enjoy it. It is our friend,
our babysitter, our companion. -

TiVo COMES TO TOWN

hen you're watching TV, do you sometimes want
LVAVE: record a programme that has already started?

Or maybe you want to watch the replay of the goal
your favourite team has just scored? Have you ever wanted to
record a programme but find that you don't have a blank videotape?
Well, TiVo is the answer to your problems. It's the latest gadget in
the TV revolution. What is it? It’s a personal video recorder (PVR),
a box that you put on top of your television set, and it means that
you can watch what you want when you want.
How do you use TiVo, the PVR? This kind of recorder doesn't use
tape; it converts television pictures into a digital format and saves
them, just as a computer does, onto a hard drive big enough to
store forty hours of programmes with DVD-style clarity.
You no longer have to set details of a recording; you simply point
your remote control at the TV screen. You will see a programme
guide and all you have to do is highlight the title of the programme
you want to record. Nothing could be easier. You can record the
programmes of an entire evening, which you can watch when you
have time.
But TiVo does much more than this. It permits you to skip the
advertising; if you have to do something urgent, you can pause
a live programme for
up to thirty minutes
and then return to it
without missing a
moment. If you don't
want to miss a
particular series, you
can use the “Season
Pass", which
automatically records
every episode for you.
TiVo is intelligent
enough to learn your
viewing habits. It
remembers which
shows you enjoy and

automatically records programmes that it thinks will interest you.
You can even rewind live programmes if you missed something
important.

So, is TiVo too good to be true? Possibly. You have to buy the box
and pay a monthly subscription fee. TiVo owners have found some
drawbacks. Six out of ten people with TiVo now watch more TV
and neglect other things to use their time to watch all the TV
programmes TiVo has recorded for them. Seven out of ten record
programmes every day.

TiVo's enthusiasm for recording means that you have more
programmes to watch. If you are an avid TV fan and television is
your main source of entertainment, TiVo may be the gadget for
you. It enables you to take control of your TV... but don't let it take
control of your life!

HOW RUPERT TOOK ON THE WORLD

upert Murdoch's media empire spans the globe — but how
Re: it get there? Bruce Page reveals the political deals and

ruthless drive that gave Murdoch more power and influence
than any press baron in History.

1931 Born Keith Rupert Murdoch in Melbourne on 11 March.

1952 Inherited his first newspaper, the Adelaide News, from
his father.

1953 Graduated from Worcester College, Oxford.

1956 Married Patricia Brooker, They had one child, Prudence,
in 1959 and divorced in 1960.

1967 Married trainee reporter Anna Trov of Sydney's Daily
Mirror. They had three children: Elizabeth, Lachlan and
James.

1968 Bought the News of the World in London.

1969 Bought the Sun in London.

19376 Bought the New York Post, the Village Voice and the New
York Magazine in the U.S.

1981 Took over The Times and The Sunday Times in London in
spite of monopoly legislation.

1983 Launched the world's first satellite TV channel, “Sky’.

1985 Became a U.S. citizen in order to comply with American
media ownership laws.

1987 Bought the South China Morning Post.

1992 Bought broadcasting rights for Premier League football
for £300 million.

1993 Bought “Star Television” in Asia:

1997 Bought Los Angeles Dodgers baseball team.

1998 Divorced Anna, his wife of 31 years, and married Wendy
Deng. Murdoch met the Chinese-born Deng while she
was working for Star TV. They have a daughter, Grace.

2000 Bought ten U.S. TV stations.

2003 Wendy gave birth to another child, a daughter called Chloe.

Murdoch Becomes American
MI urdoch broke into U.S. broadcasting by buying the

financially derelict Fox movie studio and seven TV stations —
then combining them. The fashion of the day was linking
movie assets with broadcasting.

Cross-ownership rules prevented
newspapers from running television

in their own location. Murdoch said he

A more serious problem was linked

to the basic design of American
television. To prevent concentration

of power, American television had a
subdivided structure, with hundreds
of locally owned stations. Most of these stations could not afford
to make their own drama, soaps and news: they had to buy them.
To maintain subdivision, limits were set on the number of stations
a company could control. But Murdoch was already practised

in accepting the explicit regulations and eroding them by implicit
practice.

But beyond was a much larger point. American media law said that
anyone controlling more than 25% of a television system had to be
a U.S. citizen. “Not a problem,” said Murdoch. He held a green
card issued by the U.S. Immigration Service, but just as a
necessity of working for Australia in America. He had always

Murdoch and China

urdoch took.on China in 1993 when he paid $525 million
to take control of Satellite Television Asia Region (Star TV)

based in Hong Kong. Three months after acquiring Star,
Murdoch gave a speech in London in which he suggested his
satellites would soon eliminate totalitarian politics throughout

Advances in the technology of communications have proved an
unambiguous threat to totalitarian regimes: fax machines enable
dissidents to by-pass state-controlled print media; direct-dial
telephone makes it difficult for a state to control interpersonal
voice communication; and satellite broadcasting makes it possible
for residents of many closed societies to by-pass state-controlled
television channels.

en Margaret Thatcher's government was dying, both

LV AV Atos Sky system and its rival British Satellite

Murdoch managed to do the merger. Since then, Sky has been
